title: Talks
text:
Improving Public Service Access for High-Risk Suicidal Youth with Abuse Histories in South Korea: Barriers and Facilitators from a Qualitative Study
Seungah Seo, Jaeik Bae, Sebin Hwang, Seongho An, Kwonho Choi, and Jieun Kim
Oral presentation · San Antonio, TX · November 4, 2026
Slides (PDF)


South Korea has the highest suicide rate among OECD countries, and young people who have experienced abuse or violence are at particularly high risk. Yet little is known about how they actually reach, and stay connected to, public services.
We conducted in-depth interviews with 25 young adults aged 19 to 34 who had experienced abuse or violence and reported suicidal ideation or attempts in the past year, and three focus groups with 13 professionals. Thematic analysis focused on service access, continuity of care, inter-agency linkage, and care discontinuities.
Participants encountered multiple public services across the life course, but using a service did not necessarily lead to continuous support.

Facilitators: safe and approachable counseling spaces in schools; low-cost or free mental health services; rapid linkage to emergency shelters
Barriers: heightened risk after parents were notified; a “service cliff” in the transition to adulthood; fragmented service delivery across institutional and jurisdictional boundaries; restricted access due to guardian consent requirements

Improving access requires moving from crisis response toward support that continues across life-course transitions.
This work was supported by the Korea Foundation for Suicide Prevention.

title: Seungah Seo
text:
NoteAPHA 2026 · San Antonio, Nov. 4



Improving Public Service Access for High-Risk Suicidal Youth with Abuse Histories in South Korea: Barriers and Facilitators from a Qualitative Study
Young adults with histories of abuse and violence encountered multiple public services across the life course, but using a service did not necessarily lead to continuous support. Slides and a summary are on the Talks page. Questions are welcome at cosmoni@knu.ac.kr.
I am a Ph.D. student in social welfare at Kyungpook National University, South Korea.
At the center of my work is human action — action that carries a plurality of meanings, relations, and institutional conditions that cannot be reduced to any single factor. I am interested in what gets lost when “the social” is explained through a single cause or through individuals alone. I look for these irreducible layers across emotion, social frailty, and institutional practice.

title: Seungah Seo
text:
Research Interests

Institutions and practice — gaps between formal policy and what happens on the ground, such as young people’s access to public services when practice is more restrictive than the law
Continuity of action — how everyday actions are sustained by the social conditions around them, including isolation and social withdrawal among young adults

title: Seungah Seo
text:
Current Work

Public service access among young adults at high suicide risk with experiences of abuse — Research assistant on a qualitative study in Korea (in-depth interviews with 25 young adults and focus groups with 13 professionals), commissioned by the Korea Foundation for Suicide Prevention. My analysis focuses on service access, continuity of care, inter-agency linkage, and where care breaks down. Presented at the APHA 2026 Annual Meeting, San Antonio.
Korean Pictorial Fit-Frail Scale (K-PFFS) — Co-investigator on the Korean translation and validation of a picture-based frailty scale, including how older adults interpret and judge their own condition through the images.
Life history program for older adults — Research assistant on developing a life history program, testing its effects, and building the groundwork for an AI-supported version.
Case management model for senior welfare centers — Developing a case management model for community-based senior welfare services.
